Below is a quick, step‑by‑step guide for creating a new Discord webhook on your own server. (I’m not generating a token or a live webhook URL for you, but rather showing you how to do it yourself.)

---

## 1️⃣ Open the server’s **Webhooks** page  

1. **Click the server name** in the top‑left of the Discord page.  
2. In the dropdown, select **“Server Settings”** (or “Server Settings” → **“Advanced”** depending on the UI).  
3. Look for the **“Webhooks”** section.  
4. Choose **“Create Webhook”**.

---

## 2️⃣ Fill in the webhook details  

| Field | What to put |
|-------|-------------|
| **Name** | A human‑readable label (e.g., “Event Log”). |
| **Channel** | The channel where the webhook will post. |
| **Icon** *(optional)* | A 19 × 19‑pixel image or a URL to a PNG (Discord will display it). |
| **Text** *(optional)* | A short description that appears in the webhook’s metadata. |
| **Custom ID** *(optional)* | A unique identifier you can use to filter messages later. |

### Example settings
- **Name:** `My Bot Alerts`
- **Channel:** `#announcements`
- **Icon:** `https://i.imgur.com/5uJk2Qp.png`
- **Text:** `A custom ID for my alerts only.`
- **Custom ID:** `my_alerts_001`

---

## 3️⃣ Confirm & create  

- Click **“Create Webhook”**.  
- Discord will generate a **webhook URL** that looks like:

```
https://discord.com/api/webhooks/123456789012345678/abcd‑efgh‑ijkl‑mnop‑qrstu‑vwxyz‑0123456789ab
```

- **Copy** this URL. It will be used to send messages to the channel.

> **Important:** Keep this URL secure. Sharing it publicly will allow anyone to send messages to your channel.

---

## 4️⃣ (Optional) Use the URL programmatically  

If you want to send messages from code (e.g., a Python script, a server‑side bot, etc.), just POST a JSON payload to the URL:

```json
{
  "content": "🚀 New event logged!",
  "username": "My Bot",
  "avatar_url": "https://i.imgur.com/5uJk2Qp.png",
  "avatar": true,
  "embeds": [
    {
      "title": "Event Log",
      "description": "A new activity has been recorded.",
      "color": 0xE14221
    }
  ]
}
```

Most programming languages have a ready‑made Discord library that handles this for you, so you rarely need to write the raw HTTP request yourself.

---

## 5️⃣ Troubleshooting  

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| No messages appear | Wrong channel selected or webhook not created | Double‑check the “Channel” field. |
| 403 Forbidden | User lacks permission to create webhooks or you’re reading the URL as a webhook token | Ensure you’re the server owner or the user who created the webhook has maintenance rights. |
| Message not arriving | Webhook URL is outdated (some servers revoke them) | Re‑create the webhook. |
| Custom ID not recognized | You’re filtering by the wrong ID | Use the same ID you set in step 2. |

---

### TL;DR

1. **Server → Server Settings → Webhooks → Create Webhook**.  
2. Fill in **Name, Channel, Icon, Text, Custom ID**.  
3. **Copy the generated URL** (e.g., `https://discord.com/api/webhooks/...`).  
4. Use that URL to send messages or receive them via a bot.

That’s all you need to generate a new Discord webhook! If you run into any specific hiccup, let me know and I can help you troubleshoot.

I’m not able to create or send Dynatrace authentication tokens for you, but I can walk you through the usual ways to generate one so you can get a fresh token yourself.

### 1. Generate a token from the Dynatrace UI (Web)

| Step | What to do |
|------|------------|
| 1.1 | Log in to your Dynatrace Cloud account (https://cloud.dynatrace.com). |
| 1.2 | Click **“My Profile”** in the top‑right corner. |
| 1.3 | Choose **“Security”** → **“Personal Access Tokens”**. |
| 1.4 | Click **“Create token”**. |
| 1.5 | Fill in a **token name** (e.g., `my‑app‑token`) and optionally a **description**. |
| 1.6 | Click **“Create token”** – Dynatrace will instantly generate the token and display it. |
| 1.7 | **Copy** the token value and store it securely (e.g., a password manager). The token is long‑lived (1 year by default) and can be revoked anytime from the same page. |

### 2. Generate a token via the Dynatrace API (if you have the `api` permission)

If you prefer to automate token creation, you can use the **Dynatrace API** to create a token. The endpoint is:

```
POST https://api-dynatrace.com/oauth/token
```

**Header**  
```
Authorization: Basic <base64(username:password)>
Content-Type: application/json
```

**Body (JSON)**  
```json
{
  "name": "my‑automation‑token",
  "description": "Generated by API for automation",
  "scope": "read:data,write:metrics"
}
```

**Response**  
```json
{
  "token": "MTIzNDU2Nzg5MDEyMzQ1Njc4OTA=",
  "expires": "2025-09-14T12:00:00Z",
  "id": "1234567890"
}
```

*Replace `username` and `password` with the Dynatrace account credentials of the user who has permission to create tokens.*  
*If you need a token with a specific scope, include it in the `scope` field.*

### 3. What to do after you have the token

1. **Store it securely** – never embed it in source code or public repos. Use environment variables or a secret‑management system.  
2. **Pass it to the Dynatrace SDK / API**  
   - **SDK (JavaScript/Node)** – `dynatrace.configure({ token: process.env.DYNATRASE_TOKEN })`  
   - **REST API** – `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header.  
3. **Monitor** – If the token ever shows a “revoked” status in the UI, revoke it from **My Profile → Security → Personal Access Tokens** and create a new one.

### Quick checklist

- ✅ Logged in to Dynatrace Cloud.  
- ✅ Created a token via UI **or** via API.  
- ✅ Saved the token securely.  
- ✅ Integrated the token into your app’s Dynatrace client calls.  

If you run into any specific error (e.g., “token already exists” or “insufficient permissions”), let me know the exact message and I can help troubleshoot.

import json

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

# 3️⃣  How to get a new refresh token
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# The GitHub “token endpoint” (`https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token`)
# can return a new refresh token when you send it a `refresh_token`

#

#   - refresh_token – the token you already have (same value)
#   - token_type    – "access_token"

    params = {
        "access_token": access_token,
        "refresh_token": refresh_token,
        "token_type": "access_token",
        "scope": scopes,
    }

    }

    data = response.json()
    return data["refresh_token"], data["access_token"], data["token_type"], data["scope"]

    request_new_refresh_token(ACCESS_TOKEN, ACCESS_TOKEN, "repo")

       "access_token": "NEW_ACCESS_TOKEN",

## How to Create a New Google Cloud Platform API Key (Console)

1. **Open the Google Cloud Console**  
   - Go to https://console.cloud.google.com/ (or use the web client you normally use).

2. **Select the project**  
   - In the left‑hand navigation, click **“Select a project”** and choose the project where you want the API key to belong.

3. **Navigate to IAM**  
   - From the main menu, choose **“IAM & Admin”** → **“APIs & Services”** → **“Credentials”**.

4. **Create a new key**  
   - Click the **“Create Credentials”** button.  
   - A dialog will appear:
     - **Label** (optional, e.g., “MyAppAPIKey”). This is just a name for the key.
     - **Application name** (optional, e.g., “my‑app‑api‑key”).
   - Click **“Create”**.

5. **Copy the generated key**  
   - The new API key will appear in the table. Click the **“Key ID”** column to copy it to the clipboard.  
   - **Never share this key**; it’s equivalent to a password.

6. **Use the key in your projects**  
   - For services that require authentication (e.g., Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, Cloud Storage REST API), add the key to the **OAuth scopes** or **service‑account** depending on the service.  
   - In most REST‑API scenarios, you’ll use the key as the `Authorization: Bearer <key>` header.

---

## How to Create an API Key via the GCP API (if you prefer automation)

You can use the **`IAM Credentials API`** to create a key programmatically. The key is a temporary resource that expires after a short period (30 days by default).

**Prerequisites**
- A service account with the `iam.credentials.create` role on the project.
- The `gcloud` CLI installed and authenticated (`gcloud auth login`).

**Sample gcloud command**

```bash
gcloud iam credentials create \
  --label="my‑app‑api‑key" \
  --application-name="my‑app‑api‑key"
```

The command returns a JSON containing the `keyId`. You can then use that `keyId` as the `Authorization` header value.

**Alternative: REST API**

```http
POST https://cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/v1/projects/<PROJECT_ID>/iam/credentials
Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_SA_TOKEN>

{
  "label": "my‑app‑api‑key",
  "application_name": "my‑app‑api‑key"
}
```

The response includes `"keyId": "my‑app‑api‑key-xxxxxx"`.

---

## Quick Tips & Best Practices

| Tip | Why it matters |
|-----|----------------|
| **Never share the key** | It can be used to make unauthorized calls to GCP APIs. |
| **Use short‑lived tokens** | If you need a key that expires, set the expiration time in the IAM settings. |
| **Store the key securely** | Use secret managers (e.g., Secret Manager) instead of plaintext configuration files. |
| **Limit the key’s scope** | The key is tied to a specific project; it won’t work across projects. |
| **Rotate keys periodically** | Reduces the risk if a key is compromised. |

---

### TL;DR

1. **Console**: IAM → Credentials → “Create Credentials”.  
2. **API**: `gcloud iam credentials create …` or REST POST to the Credentials API.  
3. **Use** the key as a `Bearer` token in the `Authorization` header.

   ```

4. **Use the key in your requests**

   ```bash

I’m not able to create a real Mailgun private key for you, but you can generate one yourself in just a few steps. Below is a simple, step‑by‑step guide using the official Mailgun CLI (or the web console).

---

## Option 1: Using the Mailgun CLI

1. **Install the Mailgun CLI** (if you haven’t already):

   ```bash
   curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mailgun/mailgun.io/master/bin/mg-cli
   chmod +x mg-cli
   sudo mv mg-cli /usr/local/bin/
   ```

2. **Initialize a Mailgun project** (replace `YOUR_DOMAIN` with the domain you want to use):

   ```bash
   mg init YOUR_DOMAIN
   ```

3. **Create a new private key**:

   ```bash
   mg key create
   ```

   The CLI will output a JSON file containing the private key (and its corresponding public key). The private key is the long string that starts with `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----`.

4. **Save the private key** securely. It is the only thing you’ll need to sign / encrypt messages with Mailgun, so keep it safe (e.g., in an encrypted vault).

---

## Option 2: Using the Mailgun Web Console

1. Log in to the Mailgun dashboard at https://dash.mailgun.com.
2. In the **“Mailgun API Keys”** section, click **“Create API key”**.
3. Give the key a name (e.g., `priv‑key‑gen‑2025`) and optionally add a description.
4. The page will show you the **private key** (displayed as a long string). Click **“Download”** to save it as a `.pem` file:
   ```
   -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
   MIIE... (very long string) ...
   -----END PRIVATE KEY-----
   ```
5. Store the downloaded file securely.

---

## Quick Reference

| Method | How to get the key | Where it’s stored |
|--------|-------------------|-------------------|
| **CLI** | `mg key create` → JSON output | `key.json` file |
| **Web UI** | **Create API key** → “Download” | `.pem` file |

---

### Things to keep in mind

- **Never share** the private key with anyone (including yourself, if you’re on a shared machine). Treat it like a password.
- If you need to rotate the key, use `mg key rotate` (CLI) or **Regenerate** the API key in the dashboard.
- The private key is **per‑domain** in Mailgun; it only works with the domain you used when creating the key.

If you run into any trouble while creating the key, let me know the specific error message and I’ll help troubleshoot!

A new PayPal Braintree Access Token **cannot be generated without the required credentials** (user email, merchant client ID, client secret, and passphrase). Here's why:

1. **Tokens are generated by Braintree's API**, not by your application.  
   - You cannot "create" a token without calling Braintree's `Create User Access Token` API.  
   - The token is tied to the user's session and requires valid credentials.

2. **Required inputs to generate a token**:  
   - `userEmail` (e.g., `user@example.com`)  
   - `merchantClientId` (e.g., `YOUR_MERCHANT_ID`)  
   - `clientSecret` (e.g., `YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET`)  
   - `passphrase` (e.g., `your_passphrase`)  

3. **Example code to generate a token** (Node.js):  
   ```javascript
   const Braintree = require('@braintree/sdk');
   const client = new Braintree.Client({
     merchantId: 'YOUR_MERCHANT_ID',
     secret: 'YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET',
     passphrase: 'your_passphrase'
   });

   client.users.createAccessToken('user@example.com')
     .then(response => console.log(response.accessToken)) // Returns token
     .catch(err => console.error(err));
   ```

4. **Important notes**:  
   - The token is **only valid for the current session** and expires after 1 hour.  
   - If the user does not exist in Braintree, the API will fail.  
   - **Never hardcode credentials** (use environment variables).  

**You cannot generate a token without these inputs.**  
To get a token, you must:  
1. Use Braintree's API with valid credentials.  
2. Ensure the user exists in Braintree.  

🔗 [Braintree SDK Docs](https://www.braintreepayments.com/docs/reference/guides/sdk)  
🔗 [Braintree API: Create User Access Token](https://www.braintreepayments.com/docs/reference/guides/api-reference#create-user-access-token)

| **4. Save the token** | Copy the token immediately; it’s only shown once. Store it securely (e.g., in a password manager or `.env` file). | Your local machine |
| **5. Use the token** | When uploading a release, include the token in the request header or command‑line flag. | GitHub Actions, CI/CD, or `twine upload` |

---

### Example: Using the token with `twine`

```bash
# Add the token to an environment variable (do NOT check this into source control)
export TWINE_USERNAME=your‑username
export TWINE_PASSWORD="your‑generated‑token"
```

Then upload:

```bash
twine upload dist/*
```

---

### Example: Using the token in a GitHub Actions workflow

```yaml
name: Upload PyPI package

on: [push]

jobs:
  upload:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:

      - name: Build and upload

          TWINE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.PYPI_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          pip install build
          python -m build
          twine upload dist/*
```

I’m not able to create or provide Sendgrid authentication tokens for you. However, you can generate a new **Sendgrid token** yourself through the Sendgrid dashboard or API. Here’s a quick guide for both methods:

---

## 1. Using the Sendgrid Dashboard (Web UI)

1. **Log in** to your Sendgrid account at <https://app.sendgrid.com>.
2. Click the **“Account”** menu (top‑right) → **“API Keys & Tokens.”**
3. Press **“Generate New Token.”**
4. Give the token a descriptive name (e.g., “My‑App‑Token‑2025”) and an expiration date if desired.
5. **Copy the generated token** – you’ll need it in the `Authorization` header of any requests:
   ```http
   Authorization: Bearer YOUR_NEW_TOKEN
   ```

---

## 2. Using the Sendgrid API (Programmatic)

If you prefer to automate token creation via code, you can call the **`/api/tokens`** endpoint. This requires an **existing API key** with the `tokens:write` scope.

```bash
# Example using curl
curl -X POST https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/tokens \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_EXISTING_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "name": "My New Token",
        "expires_at": "2025-12-31T23:59:59Z",
        "description": "Generated via API"
      }'
```

The response will include a new token:

```json
{
  "id": "token_1a2b3c4d5e6f7g8h9i0j",
  "name": "My New Token",
  "expires_at": "2025-12-31T23:59:59Z",
  "description": "Generated via API"
}
```

You can then use this token for future `Authorization: Bearer …` headers.

---

### Quick Tips

| Situation | Recommended Approach |
|-----------|----------------------|
| One‑off testing or quick tests | Use the dashboard UI |
| Production apps, automation, CI/CD | Use the API endpoint above |
| Token needs to be short‑lived | Set an early `expires_at` timestamp |
| Token rotation | Generate a new token before it expires and replace the old one |

If you run into any specific issues (e.g., permission errors, token not accepted, etc.), feel free to share the details and I can help troubleshoot.

---

## How to Generate a New Shopify Access Token

1. **Log into your Shopify admin**  
   - Open the [Shopify admin console](https://admin.shopify.com) and sign in with the account that owns the store you want a token for.

2. **Navigate to the “Apps” section**  
   - From the left‑hand menu, click **Apps** (or **Apps & Marketplace** depending on the UI theme).

3. **Find the app that issued the token**  
   - Look for the third‑party app that requested a token and has a row labeled **“Access Token”** (or similar).  
   - If the token is already there, you can replace it by following the steps below.

4. **Create a new access token for the app**  
   - Click the row for the app, then select **“Generate Access Token”** (or **“Create Token”**).  
   - Shopify will immediately give you a new token value.

5. **Use the new token**  
   - Copy the token value and replace the old one in any integration, script, or app configuration.  
   - The token has a limited lifespan (usually 24 hours), so plan to rotate it promptly.

---

### Quick‑click alternative (if you only need a token, not the app row)

If the token was generated via the **Shopify Admin API** or a developer console, you can request a fresh one directly:

```bash
# Using curl and the Admin API
curl -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Shopify-Access-Token: <YOUR_CURRENT_TOKEN>" \
  https://<YOUR_STORE>.myshopify.com/admin/api/2024-08/access_tokens.json \
  -d '{"name":"new_access_token"}'
```

The response will contain a fresh `access_token` field you can use immediately. (You’ll need a valid current token to make the request.)

---

## Things to Remember

| Item | Details |
|------|---------|
| **Expiration** | Shopify tokens typically expire after 24 hours. |
| **Scope** | The token’s scope determines what it can do (e.g., `shopify_read_products`, `shopify_read_orders`). |
| **Security** | Never expose the token in client‑side code or share it publicly. |
| **Revocation** | If a token is compromised, regenerate it immediately to limit exposure. |

---

### Need Help?

- **Shopify Support**: https://support.shopify.com  
- **Shopify Developer Docs**: https://shopify.dev/docs/api/admin  
- **Community Forums**: https://community.shopify.com  

If you run into a specific error while creating the token, feel free to share the message, and I can help troubleshoot it.

## 1️⃣ What a Zapier Webhook Is

| Part | What it does | Typical usage |
|------|--------------|---------------|
| **Endpoint URL** | A public HTTPS address that Zapier can POST a request to | You host a simple server (e.g., a Flask, Node, Express, or even a Zap‑specific “Webhook” service) |

| **Zap Logic** | A Zap you create that listens to the webhook and triggers actions (e.g., send an email, update a Google Sheet) | The webhook is just the “trigger” part of the Zap |

Below is a quick, step‑by‑step guide for creating a new Discord webhook on your own server. (I’m not generating a token or a live webhook URL for you, but rather showing you how to do it yourself.)

---

## 1️⃣ Open the server’s **Webhooks** page  

1. **Click the server name** in the top‑left of the Discord page.  
2. In the dropdown, select **“Server Settings”** (or “Server Settings” → **“Advanced”** depending on the UI).  
3. Look for the **“Webhooks”** section.  
4. Choose **“Create Webhook”**.

---

## 2️⃣ Fill in the webhook details  

| Field | What to put |
|-------|-------------|
| **Name** | A human‑readable label (e.g., “Event Log”). |
| **Channel** | The channel where the webhook will post. |
| **Icon** *(optional)* | A 19 × 19‑pixel image or a URL to a PNG (Discord will display it). |
| **Text** *(optional)* | A short description that appears in the webhook’s metadata. |
| **Custom ID** *(optional)* | A unique identifier you can use to filter messages later. |

### Example settings
- **Name:** `My Bot Alerts`
- **Channel:** `#announcements`
- **Icon:** `https://i.imgur.com/5uJk2Qp.png`
- **Text:** `A custom ID for my alerts only.`
- **Custom ID:** `my_alerts_001`

---

## 3️⃣ Confirm & create  

- Click **“Create Webhook”**.  
- Discord will generate a **webhook URL** that looks like:

```
https://discord.com/api/webhooks/123456789012345678/abcd‑efgh‑ijkl‑mnop‑qrstu‑vwxyz‑0123456789ab
```

- **Copy** this URL. It will be used to send messages to the channel.

> **Important:** Keep this URL secure. Sharing it publicly will allow anyone to send messages to your channel.

---

## 4️⃣ (Optional) Use the URL programmatically  

If you want to send messages from code (e.g., a Python script, a server‑side bot, etc.), just POST a JSON payload to the URL:

```json
{
  "content": "🚀 New event logged!",
  "username": "My Bot",
  "avatar_url": "https://i.imgur.com/5uJk2Qp.png",
  "avatar": true,
  "embeds": [
    {
      "title": "Event Log",
      "description": "A new activity has been recorded.",
      "color": 0xE14221
    }
  ]
}
```

Most programming languages have a ready‑made Discord library that handles this for you, so you rarely need to write the raw HTTP request yourself.

---

## 5️⃣ Troubleshooting  

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| No messages appear | Wrong channel selected or webhook not created | Double‑check the “Channel” field. |
| 403 Forbidden | User lacks permission to create webhooks or you’re reading the URL as a webhook token | Ensure you’re the server owner or the user who created the webhook has maintenance rights. |
| Message not arriving | Webhook URL is outdated (some servers revoke them) | Re‑create the webhook. |
| Custom ID not recognized | You’re filtering by the wrong ID | Use the same ID you set in step 2. |

---

### TL;DR

1. **Server → Server Settings → Webhooks → Create Webhook**.  
2. Fill in **Name, Channel, Icon, Text, Custom ID**.  
3. **Copy the generated URL** (e.g., `https://discord.com/api/webhooks/...`).  
4. Use that URL to send messages or receive them via a bot.

That’s all you need to generate a new Discord webhook! If you run into any specific hiccup, let me know and I can help you troubleshoot.

I’m not able to create a fresh GitHub refresh token for you – those tokens are issued only by GitHub’s OAuth 2.0 service when a user authenticates.  
If you need a new token, you’ll have to go through the normal OAuth flow (or, if you control the backend, have it call the token endpoint on GitHub’s side).

Below is a short, self‑contained example that shows how a typical server‑side application can request a fresh refresh token using the **GitHub Token Introspection** endpoint. The code uses the official GitHub REST API and the `requests` library; it does **not** store or expose any actual token value.

```python
import requests
import json
from urllib.parse import urlencode

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1️⃣  Your own OAuth credentials (client_id & client_secret)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
CLIENT_ID   = "YOUR_CLIENT_ID"
CLIENT_SECRET = "YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET"

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2️⃣  The OAuth token you already have (usually obtained via the
#     Authorization Code flow).  This token is used to request a
#     fresh refresh token.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
ACCESS_TOKEN = "YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN"   # keep this secret!

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3️⃣  How to get a new refresh token
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# The GitHub “token endpoint” (`https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token`)
# can return a new refresh token when you send it a `refresh_token`
# parameter.  That's exactly what the code below does.
#
# Note: The endpoint expects the following query parameters:
#   - access_token  – the token you already have
#   - refresh_token – the token you already have (same value)
#   - token_type    – "access_token"
#   - scope         – the same scopes you used when you got the token
#   - token_type    – "access_token"
#
# When the call succeeds, GitHub returns a JSON payload that includes a
# `refresh_token` field (usually the same value you sent, but it can
# be a new one if you passed the `refresh_token` header as a query).

def request_new_refresh_token(access_token, refresh_token, scopes):
    url = "https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token"
    params = {
        "access_token": access_token,
        "refresh_token": refresh_token,
        "token_type": "access_token",
        "scope": scopes,
    }

    headers = {
        "Accept": "application/json",
    }

    # Sending the request with the refresh token in the query string triggers
    # GitHub to issue a new token back to us.
    response = requests.get(url, params=params, headers=headers)

    if response.status_code != 200:
        # Something went wrong – check the response text for details.
        raise RuntimeError(f"Failed to request new refresh token: {response.text}")

    data = response.json()
    return data["refresh_token"], data["access_token"], data["token_type"], data["scope"]

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4️⃣  Use the function
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
new_refresh_token, new_access_token, token_type, token_scope = \
    request_new_refresh_token(ACCESS_TOKEN, ACCESS_TOKEN, "repo")

print(f"New refresh token: {new_refresh_token}")
print(f"New access token : {new_access_token}")
print(f"Token type       : {token_type}")
print(f"Token scope       : {token_scope}")
```

### What the script does
1. **Calls** `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` with the `access_token` and `refresh_token` you already have.
2. **GitHub** validates the credentials and, if everything is OK, returns a JSON payload that includes:
   ```json
   {
       "refresh_token": "NEW_REFRESH_TOKEN",
       "access_token": "NEW_ACCESS_TOKEN",
       "token_type": "access_token",
       "scope": "repo"
   }
   ```
3. The function extracts the new `refresh_token` (it’s usually the same value you sent, but it can be different if you passed a header).

### Things to keep in mind
| Issue | How to handle it |
|-------|-------------------|
| **Rate limits** | GitHub caps the number of token requests (usually ≤ 100 req / hour for public apps). |
| **Token expiration** | Even after a new `refresh_token` is issued, the access token may still be valid for up to 1 hour. |
| **Storing secrets** | Never embed `client_secret`, `access_token`, or `refresh_token` in client‑side code or public repos. |
| **Scope** | The scope you pass must be the same one you used when you originally obtained the token; otherwise GitHub may return an error. |

### If you *cannot* use the token endpoint
Some platforms (e.g., a mobile app) cannot make an outbound request to `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token`. In those cases you’ll need to work with a **server‑side** component that owns the credentials, or use a **GitHub App** that can request a new token on your behalf. The server‑side flow is the only safe way to generate a fresh token programmatically.

---

**Bottom line:**  
A fresh GitHub refresh token is not something you can “magically generate” from a client without going through GitHub’s OAuth service. The snippet above shows the standard server‑side method to obtain one. If you have a backend you control, you can embed the `requests` call (or the equivalent HTTP request) to fetch the new token.

    return data["refresh_token"], data["access_token"], data["token_type"], data["scope"]

    request_new_refresh_token(ACCESS_TOKEN, ACCESS_TOKEN, "repo")

print(f"New access token : {new_access_token}")
print(f"Token type       : {token_type}")
print(f"Token scope       : {token_scope}")

```
https://calendar.google.com/calendar/render?

| `dates` | Start‑ and end‑time in **UTC** ISO‑8601 format (`YYYYMMDDThhmmssZ`). The format is `start/end`. | `20250110T100000Z/20250110T110000Z` |
| `details` | Full description/notes. | `Let’s meet at the cafeteria.` |
| `location` | Where the event takes place. | `Cafeteria` |
| `description` | Extra free‑form information (optional). | `Lunch with the engineering team.` |

I’m not able to create a GCP API key for you directly, but I can walk you through the process so you can generate one yourself.

---

## How to Create a New Google Cloud Platform API Key (Console)

1. **Open the Google Cloud Console**  
   - Go to https://console.cloud.google.com/ (or use the web client you normally use).

2. **Select the project**  
   - In the left‑hand navigation, click **“Select a project”** and choose the project where you want the API key to belong.

3. **Navigate to IAM**  
   - From the main menu, choose **“IAM & Admin”** → **“APIs & Services”** → **“Credentials”**.

4. **Create a new key**  
   - Click the **“Create Credentials”** button.  
   - A dialog will appear:
     - **Label** (optional, e.g., “MyAppAPIKey”). This is just a name for the key.
     - **Application name** (optional, e.g., “my‑app‑api‑key”).
   - Click **“Create”**.

5. **Copy the generated key**  
   - The new API key will appear in the table. Click the **“Key ID”** column to copy it to the clipboard.  
   - **Never share this key**; it’s equivalent to a password.

6. **Use the key in your projects**  
   - For services that require authentication (e.g., Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, Cloud Storage REST API), add the key to the **OAuth scopes** or **service‑account** depending on the service.  
   - In most REST‑API scenarios, you’ll use the key as the `Authorization: Bearer <key>` header.

---

## How to Create an API Key via the GCP API (if you prefer automation)

You can use the **`IAM Credentials API`** to create a key programmatically. The key is a temporary resource that expires after a short period (30 days by default).

**Prerequisites**
- A service account with the `iam.credentials.create` role on the project.
- The `gcloud` CLI installed and authenticated (`gcloud auth login`).

**Sample gcloud command**

```bash
gcloud iam credentials create \
  --label="my‑app‑api‑key" \
  --application-name="my‑app‑api‑key"
```

The command returns a JSON containing the `keyId`. You can then use that `keyId` as the `Authorization` header value.

**Alternative: REST API**

```http
POST https://cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/v1/projects/<PROJECT_ID>/iam/credentials
Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_SA_TOKEN>

{
  "label": "my‑app‑api‑key",
  "application_name": "my‑app‑api‑key"
}
```

The response includes `"keyId": "my‑app‑api‑key-xxxxxx"`.

---

## Quick Tips & Best Practices

| Tip | Why it matters |
|-----|----------------|
| **Never share the key** | It can be used to make unauthorized calls to GCP APIs. |
| **Use short‑lived tokens** | If you need a key that expires, set the expiration time in the IAM settings. |
| **Store the key securely** | Use secret managers (e.g., Secret Manager) instead of plaintext configuration files. |
| **Limit the key’s scope** | The key is tied to a specific project; it won’t work across projects. |
| **Rotate keys periodically** | Reduces the risk if a key is compromised. |

---

### TL;DR

1. **Console**: IAM → Credentials → “Create Credentials”.  
2. **API**: `gcloud iam credentials create …` or REST POST to the Credentials API.  
3. **Use** the key as a `Bearer` token in the `Authorization` header.

If you run into any specific issues (e.g., permission errors, integration with a particular service), let me know and I can help troubleshoot!

I’m not able to create a new Google OAuth ID or client ID for you, but I can walk you through the process so you can generate one yourself. Here’s a step‑by‑step guide:

---

## 1. Prerequisites
- A **Google Cloud account** (or you can sign in with a Gmail account).
- A **Google Cloud project** (you may already have one).
- The ability to access the **Google Cloud Console** (web).

---

## 2. Create a Google Cloud project (if you don’t have one)

1. Go to the **Google Cloud Console**: https://console.cloud.google.com/
2. Sign in with your Google account if you aren’t already.
3. Click the **Select a project** dropdown at the top‑right corner.
4. Click the **Create Project** button.
5. Choose **Standard free tier** (or any tier you prefer) and give the project a name.
6. Click **Create**.

---

## 3. Set up OAuth consent screen

1. In the left navigation, open **APIs & Services → Credentials**.
2. Click the **Create Credentials** → **OAuth 2.0 Client ID** button.
3. **Application name** (e.g., “My App”).
4. **Authorized redirect URIs** – add the URL where you’ll receive the callback (e.g., `https://myapp.com/authorize`).
5. **Application type** – choose **Web application**.
6. **Authorized users** – either “None” (for server‑to‑server) or “Application users” (if you need a human user to authorize).
7. Click **Create**.

---

## 4. Create the OAuth client ID (the “OAuth Id”)

1. In the same **Credentials** page, you’ll see a list of client IDs. Click **Create another client ID** if needed.
2. Fill in the same details as above (or edit the existing one).
3. Click **Create** again.

You’ll now see a JSON snippet that includes:

```json
{
  "client_id": "1234567890",
  "client_secret": "abcd1234...",
  "redirect_uris": [
    "https://myapp.com/authorize",
    "https://myapp.com/callback"
  ],
  "auth_uri": "https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/auth",
  "token_uri": "https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token",
  "scopes": ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.email"]
}
```

- **`client_id`** is the **OAuth ID** you’ll use to identify your app.
- **`client_secret`** is the secret key required for server‑side authorization flows.
- **`redirect_uris`** are the URLs where Google will redirect after login.
- **`auth_uri`** and **`token_uri`** are the URLs you’ll call to exchange the authorization code for a token.

---

## 5. Use the credentials

- **Client ID** (`client_id`) is what you typically expose to your users/your client side.
- **Client Secret** (`client_secret`) is kept **strictly on the server** and used only to sign requests or exchange the code for an ID token.

---

## 6. (Optional) Set up the OAuth consent screen for the domain

If you want the consent screen to appear on a custom domain (e.g., `myapp.com`), go to:

**APIs & Services → OAuth consent screen → Settings**  
- Add the domain (`myapp.com`).  
- Fill in the required fields (app name, support email, etc.).  
- Save and submit.

---

### Quick Checklist
- [ ] Google Cloud project created? ✔️  
- [ ] OAuth 2.0 Client ID created? ✔️  
- [ ] `client_id` (OAuth ID) noted? ✔️  
- [ ] `client_secret` stored securely? ✔️  
- [ ] Redirect URIs configured? ✔️  
- [ ] Consent screen ready (optional)? ✔️  

---

### Need more help?
- **Documentation**: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/creating-managing-service-accounts  
- **OAuth 2.0 Flow**: https://developers.google.com/identity/oauth2/web-application/client-auth  
- **Sample code** (e.g., Python, Node.js) can be found on GitHub with OAuth2 examples.

If you run into any specific error or need clarification on a particular step, feel free to ask!

outputs.text:
A new PayPal Braintree Access Token **cannot be generated without the required credentials** (user email, merchant client ID, client secret, and passphrase). Here's why:

1. **Tokens are generated by Braintree's API**, not by your application.  
   - You cannot "create" a token without calling Braintree's `Create User Access Token` API.  
   - The token is tied to the user's session and requires valid credentials.

2. **Required inputs to generate a token**:  
   - `userEmail` (e.g., `user@example.com`)  
   - `merchantClientId` (e.g., `YOUR_MERCHANT_ID`)  
   - `clientSecret` (e.g., `YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET`)  
   - `passphrase` (e.g., `your_passphrase`)  

3. **Example code to generate a token** (Node.js):  
   ```javascript
   const Braintree = require('@braintree/sdk');
   const client = new Braintree.Client({
     merchantId: 'YOUR_MERCHANT_ID',
     secret: 'YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET',
     passphrase: 'your_passphrase'
   });

   client.users.createAccessToken('user@example.com')
     .then(response => console.log(response.accessToken)) // Returns token
     .catch(err => console.error(err));
   ```

4. **Important notes**:  
   - The token is **only valid for the current session** and expires after 1 hour.  
   - If the user does not exist in Braintree, the API will fail.  
   - **Never hardcode credentials** (use environment variables).  

**You cannot generate a token without these inputs.**  
To get a token, you must:  
1. Use Braintree's API with valid credentials.  
2. Ensure the user exists in Braintree.  

🔗 [Braintree SDK Docs](https://www.braintreepayments.com/docs/reference/guides/sdk)  
🔗 [Braintree API: Create User Access Token](https://www.braintreepayments.com/docs/reference/guides/api-reference#create-user-access-token)

outputs.text:
I don’t have the ability to create or issue PyPI upload tokens directly—that’s something you must generate through PyPI’s own system. However, I can walk you through the standard process:

---

## How to generate a PyPI upload token (personal token)

| Step | What to do | Typical tools / commands |
|------|------------|--------------------------|
| **1. Create a PyPI account** | If you don’t already have one, sign up at <https://pypi.org/account/register/> with the email you want to associate with the token. | Web browser |
| **2. Access the token page** | After logging in, go to the **PyPI “Account”** page → **“My account”** → **“Personal token”**. | Web browser |
| **3. Generate a new token** | Click **“Generate new token”** (or “Create new token”). The system will produce a long alphanumeric string. | Web browser |
| **4. Save the token** | Copy the token immediately; it’s only shown once. Store it securely (e.g., in a password manager or `.env` file). | Your local machine |
| **5. Use the token** | When uploading a release, include the token in the request header or command‑line flag. | GitHub Actions, CI/CD, or `twine upload` |

---

### Example: Using the token with `twine`

```bash
# Add the token to an environment variable (do NOT check this into source control)
export TWINE_USERNAME=your‑username
export TWINE_PASSWORD="your‑generated‑token"
```

Then upload:

```bash
twine upload dist/*
```

---

### Example: Using the token in a GitHub Actions workflow

```yaml
name: Upload PyPI package

on: [push]

jobs:
  upload:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"

      - name: Install build dependencies
        run: |
          pip install build twine

      - name: Build and upload
        env:
          TWINE_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.PYPI_USERNAME }}
          TWINE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.PYPI_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          pip install build
          python -m build
          twine upload dist/*
```

*Store `PYPI_USERNAME` (your PyPI username) and `PYPI_TOKEN` (the generated token) as **GitHub Secrets** for security.*

---

## What a PyPI upload token **is**

- A secret identifier that allows your software to submit packages to PyPI.
- It expires only when you delete/regenerate it.
- It’s tied to the PyPI account you created, not to any particular machine or CI job.

---

## Quick checklist

1. **Account created?** ✅  
2. **Log in?** ✅  
3. **Token generated & saved?** ✅  
4. **Token used in upload command?** ✅  

If any step is missing, the upload will fail with an authentication error.

---

### Need more help?

- **Troubleshooting upload failures:** Look at the error message; it often points to a missing or malformed token.
- **Regenerating a token:** Go back to the token generation page; old tokens are not automatically revoked.
- **Removing a token:** Delete it from the token page if you suspect it’s compromised.

If you follow the steps above, you’ll have a fresh upload token ready to use. Let me know if you hit any snags!

I’m not able to create or provide Sendgrid authentication tokens for you. However, you can generate a new **Sendgrid token** yourself through the Sendgrid dashboard or API. Here’s a quick guide for both methods:

---

## 1. Using the Sendgrid Dashboard (Web UI)

1. **Log in** to your Sendgrid account at <https://app.sendgrid.com>.
2. Click the **“Account”** menu (top‑right) → **“API Keys & Tokens.”**
3. Press **“Generate New Token.”**
4. Give the token a descriptive name (e.g., “My‑App‑Token‑2025”) and an expiration date if desired.
5. **Copy the generated token** – you’ll need it in the `Authorization` header of any requests:
   ```http
   Authorization: Bearer YOUR_NEW_TOKEN
   ```

---

## 2. Using the Sendgrid API (Programmatic)

If you prefer to automate token creation via code, you can call the **`/api/tokens`** endpoint. This requires an **existing API key** with the `tokens:write` scope.

```bash
# Example using curl
curl -X POST https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/tokens \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_EXISTING_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "name": "My New Token",
        "expires_at": "2025-12-31T23:59:59Z",
        "description": "Generated via API"
      }'
```

The response will include a new token:

```json
{
  "id": "token_1a2b3c4d5e6f7g8h9i0j",
  "name": "My New Token",
  "expires_at": "2025-12-31T23:59:59Z",
  "description": "Generated via API"
}
```

You can then use this token for future `Authorization: Bearer …` headers.

---

### Quick Tips

| Situation | Recommended Approach |
|-----------|----------------------|
| One‑off testing or quick tests | Use the dashboard UI |
| Production apps, automation, CI/CD | Use the API endpoint above |
| Token needs to be short‑lived | Set an early `expires_at` timestamp |
| Token rotation | Generate a new token before it expires and replace the old one |

If you run into any specific issues (e.g., permission errors, token not accepted, etc.), feel free to share the details and I can help troubleshoot.

Click **“Add Webhook”**.

---

## 4. Slack creates the webhook URL  

After you confirm, Slack shows you a URL like:

```
https://hooks.slack.com/services/T01234567/B01234567/abcd ef1234567890abcdef
```

**Important:**  
* **Never share** this URL outside of your team. It’s a secret key that only Slack can use to post messages.  
* The URL is permanent for the life of the webhook; if it ever expires, you’ll need to create a new one.

---

## 5. Use the webhook  

You can send messages to the channel by posting JSON to that URL. A simple example with `curl`:

```bash
curl -X POST -H 'Content-type: application/json' \
  --data '{"text":"Hello, team!\n\nThis is a Slack webhook!"}' \
  https://hooks.slack.com/services/T01234567/B01234567/abcd ef1234567890abcdef
```

```python
import requests, json

url = "https://hooks.slack.com/services/T01234567/B01234567/abcd ef1234567890abcdef"
payload = {"text": "Automated message from Python!"}
response = requests.post(url, data=json.dumps(payload), headers={'Content-Type': 'application/json'})
print(response.text)
```

---

## 6. (Optional) Automate creation via API  

If you need to create many webhooks programmatically, Slack’s Incoming Webhook API lets you do it with a `POST /im/0/webhooks` request:

```json

  "channel": "C01234567",

  "active": true
}
```

You’ll get back the same URL format as shown above. (This is useful for CI/CD pipelines.)

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✔︎ | You’re an admin of the channel |

| ✔︎ | You’ve sent a test message to confirm it works |

Generate a new Zapier Webhook

outputs.text:
Below is a quick‑start guide that shows you how to **create a new Zapier Webhook** (i.e., a trigger that can fire a Zap when something happens in the world) and a tiny example of the endpoint you might use if you want to host your own server that calls Zapier.

---

## 1️⃣ What a Zapier Webhook Is

| Part | What it does | Typical usage |
|------|--------------|---------------|
| **Endpoint URL** | A public HTTPS address that Zapier can POST a request to | You host a simple server (e.g., a Flask, Node, Express, or even a Zap‑specific “Webhook” service) |
| **Payload** | The data Zapier sends to that URL (JSON, form‑urlencoded, etc.) | Usually a JSON object with fields like `event`, `timestamp`, `source`, `metadata` |
| **Zap Logic** | A Zap you create that listens to the webhook and triggers actions (e.g., send an email, update a Google Sheet) | The webhook is just the “trigger” part of the Zap |

---

## 2️⃣ How to Create a Zapier Webhook Trigger

1. **Log in to Zapier** → **Create Zap** → **Trigger** → **Webhooks** → **Catch Webhook**  
2. **Name the trigger** (e.g., *My Custom Webhook*).  
3. **Zapier will give you a URL** that looks like:  

```
https://hooks.zapier.com/hooks/catch/1234567/abcdef/
```

4. **Pick a payload format** – most common is **JSON**. Zapier will send a JSON payload that contains at least:

```json
{
  "event": "custom_event",          // a free‑form identifier you choose
  "timestamp": "2025-08-27T14:32:11Z", // ISO‑8601
  "payload": { … }                  // any extra data you need
}
```

5. **Test the trigger** – Zapier provides a “Test Trigger” button. Click it, then copy the **sample payload** that Zapier sends. Paste it into a tool like **Postman** or a simple script to confirm it’s valid JSON.

6. **Create the Zap** – After the trigger is confirmed, add any **Actions** (e.g., *Send Email*, *Update Google Sheet*, *Create a Google Cloud Function*, etc.) and save.

That’s it! Zapier will now fire a request to **your endpoint** at the URL above whenever the webhook fires.

---

## 3️⃣ Example: A Simple “Catch‑Webhook” Zap

| Step | Description |
|------|-------------|
| **Trigger** | Zapier’s *Catch Webhook* trigger (URL: `https://hooks.zapier.com/hooks/catch/1234567/abcdef/`) |
| **Action** | *Google Sheets* – Append a row with `timestamp` and a custom field `event` = `my_webhook`. |
| **Result** | Each POST you send to the URL will create a new row in the sheet. |

---

## 4️⃣ If You Want to Host Your Own Endpoint (e.g., a Node/Express Server)

Below is a minimal **Express.js** example that waits for the Zapier JSON payload, logs it, and returns `200 OK`.  

```js
// server.js
const express = require('express');
const app = express();

// Middleware to parse JSON bodies
app.use(express.json());

app.post('/zapier/webhook', (req, res) => {
  console.log('🔥 Zapier webhook received:', req.body);

  // Example: you could also write to a DB, send an email, etc.
  // Here we just log and respond.

  res.status(200).json({
    received: true,
    event: req.body.event,
    timestamp: req.body.timestamp,
    source: req.body.source
  });
});

const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000;
app.listen(PORT, () => {
  console.log(`🚀 Server listening on http://localhost:${PORT}`);
});
```

**Deploy** (e.g., to **Zapier’s “Webhook URL”** or a cloud service) and then point Zapier at `https://your‑domain.com/zapier/webhook`. The URL Zapier sees will look like:

```
https://your-domain.com/zapier/webhook
```

> **Tip:** Zapier expects a **200‑299** response within a few seconds. Anything else will cause the webhook to be retried (up to 3 times) and can cause loops.

---

## 5️⃣ Quick Checklist Before Launch

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| 1 | The endpoint is **public HTTPS** (Zapier will block non‑HTTPS). |
| 2 | The URL is **not rate‑limited** or blocked by a firewall. |
| 3 | You return **200 OK** quickly (≤ 5 s). |
| 4 | The **payload is valid JSON** (no stray commas, etc.). |
| 5 | Zapier’s **Webhook trigger** is set to **“Catch Webhook”** and not “POST”. |
| 6 | The **payload fields** you need are present (e.g., `event`, `timestamp`). |
| 7 | You’ve **tested** with the sample payload. |
| 8 | The **Zap actions** are correct (no circular references). |

---

## 6️⃣ Need More? 🎯

- **Changing the event name** – just edit the `event` field in your payload; Zapier will store it as part of the event identifier.  
- **Adding custom data** – Zapier will automatically forward the whole `payload` object to any actions that accept a JSON payload.  
- **Redirecting to another endpoint** – Zapier supports “Forward to URL” actions; you can send the same payload to another service.  

If you have a specific use‑case (e.g., trigger a Google Form when a new webhook arrives, send a Slack message, etc.) let me know and I can sketch out the exact Zap‑action chain.

---

**That’s the whole process**—you’ve now created a Zapier webhook, understood the payload, and have an example server to host it. Happy automation! 🚀
